title: How Humans Learn and Develop Expertise
theme: Learning Science, Skill Acquisition & Deliberate Practice
question: What actually makes people get better at difficult skills — and how would you know whether a development system is producing learning or only good-looking practice?

overview.text: Every organization that develops people — a surgical residency, a flight school, a consulting firm, a conservatory, a professional sports club — runs on a theory of how humans learn, whether or not anyone has written it down. That theory decides how practice is scheduled, how much coaches talk, what feedback looks like, what gets measured and who is judged to be improving. This week asks you to make that theory explicit and to test it against the evidence.

The week moves from memory to mastery. Lesson 1 establishes the distinction that organizes everything else: performance during practice is not the same as learning, and conditions that make practice look worse — retrieval, spacing, interleaving — often make learning last. Lesson 2 examines deliberate practice: a valuable description of high-quality practice, attached to a popular myth about hours, and the subject of a live dispute about how much practice explains. Lesson 3 turns to motor learning, where laboratory findings on practice schedules, feedback and attention are striking, but several shrink in applied settings or under bias correction, and two theoretical camps disagree about what is being learned. Lesson 4 covers cognitive load, the limits of transfer, the learning-styles myth and the measurement of learning.

Throughout, you will grade claims rather than collect them. Some principles are well supported; some are contested; some are plausible hypotheses; some are myths with excellent marketing. Your exercise asks you to design practice plans and see the learning–performance trade-off in action; your case puts you inside a residency program choosing between an expensive evidence-informed system and an established process its faculty trust; and your assignment asks you to build a development framework that is honest about which of its elements are research-supported and which are coaching hypotheses.

objectives: Distinguish learning from performance and design evaluations that measure retention and transfer rather than practice success.
Evaluate deliberate-practice theory and its critiques, interpreting variance-explained estimates and range restriction correctly.
Grade motor-learning principles — contextual interference, feedback frequency, attentional focus, constraints-led design — by laboratory, applied and bias-corrected evidence.
Explain cognitive load, the limits of transfer and the learning-styles myth, and individualize instruction by expertise rather than by labels.
Build an evidence-informed development framework that separates research-supported elements from coaching hypotheses.

lessons.title: Learning Is Not Performance: Memory, Retrieval and Desirable Difficulties
lessons.summary: What you see during practice is performance; learning is what survives a delay and a change of context — and the two can move in opposite directions.
objectives: Distinguish learning from performance and explain why only delayed or changed-context tests can reveal learning.
Explain retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving, and rank them by the strength of their evidence.
Diagnose a training program whose success metrics reward performance at the expense of learning.
lessons.executive: Most organizations judge training by how it looks while it happens: smooth sessions, high completion scores, confident trainees. Research on learning shows that these signals are unreliable and sometimes inverted. Conditions that make practice harder — retrieving instead of rereading, spacing sessions apart, mixing problem types — tend to depress in-session performance and improve what is retained weeks later. Learners and instructors routinely prefer the easier, less effective condition because it feels like progress. For an executive, the implication is managerial, not academic: if your dashboards measure only practice performance, you are rewarding the wrong thing. Ask for delayed and transfer measures before you judge any development program.

explore.text: Two hospitals train new nurses on the same rapid-response protocol. Hospital A runs a polished two-day course: instructors walk through the algorithm, trainees reread a laminated card, and on Friday afternoon everyone passes the checklist with near-perfect scores. Hospital B spreads the same content over three weeks. Each short session begins with trainees trying to reconstruct the algorithm from memory before they see it, and scenarios are mixed so that no one knows which emergency comes next. Hospital B’s trainees make more mistakes in their sessions and rate the course as harder and less satisfying. The scenario is hypothetical, but the pattern it describes is one of the best-documented findings in the science of learning.

Before reading on, predict: on the Friday of training, which hospital’s nurses score higher? Six weeks later, when a real alarm sounds on a night shift, which group is more likely to recall the algorithm correctly? How confident are you in each prediction?

A classic experiment makes the pattern concrete. Students read prose passages and then either restudied them or took a recall test with no feedback. On a test five minutes later, restudying won. On tests two days and one week later, the students who had been tested remembered more. The students who restudied also felt more confident about how much they would remember — confidence pointed the wrong way ([Roediger and Karpicke, 2006](R-roediger-2006-test-enhanced)).

If you predicted that Hospital A wins on Friday and Hospital B wins on the night shift, you already hold the central idea of this week. The difficulty is not knowing it; it is acting on it when every signal available during training — scores, smiles, trainee ratings, the instructor’s sense that the session went well — points the other way.

blocks.text: Memory researchers describe three processes. **Encoding** turns an experience into a memory trace. **Storage** keeps it over time. **Retrieval** brings it back when it is needed. Working memory is the small, temporary workspace in which you hold and manipulate information right now; long-term memory is the large store of what you know. Training is useful only if what is encoded today can be retrieved later, in a different place, under different pressure. A training session therefore has to be judged by what it does to future retrieval, which you cannot observe during the session itself.

understand.text: Two quantities that look like one

**Performance** is what a learner does during or immediately after practice. **Learning** is a relatively permanent change in capability that supports retention (doing it later) and transfer (doing it in new conditions). Soderstrom and Bjork’s integrative review shows that the distinction runs through decades of research in animal learning, motor learning and verbal learning: learning can occur without visible gains in performance, performance gains can fail to produce learning, and some manipulations push the two in opposite directions ([Soderstrom and Bjork, 2015](R-soderstrom-2015-learning)).

A useful way to picture this, developed in Bjork’s research program and discussed in the review, separates how well something is stored from how easily it can be retrieved at this moment. Practice that makes retrieval easy right now — repeating the same thing, rereading, being told the answer — produces high current performance but adds relatively little to durable storage. Practice that makes retrieval effortful, but still successful, does more to strengthen what remains available later ([Soderstrom and Bjork, 2015](R-soderstrom-2015-learning)).

understand.text: Desirable difficulties and the evidence behind each

“Desirable difficulties” is the label for conditions that slow down or complicate acquisition yet improve retention and transfer. The best-supported are retrieval practice and spacing. In a long review of ten study techniques, Dunlosky and colleagues rated practice testing and distributed practice as having high utility; interleaved practice, elaborative interrogation and self-explanation as moderate; and summarization, highlighting, the keyword mnemonic, imagery for text and rereading as low ([Dunlosky et al., 2013](R-dunlosky-2013-improving)).

understand.text: The ratings come with an important boundary. The review concerns academic material — facts, concepts and problem solving — and its strongest conclusions apply to knowledge that must be retrieved later ([Dunlosky et al., 2013](R-dunlosky-2013-improving)). Motor skills have their own literature, which shows the same learning–performance pattern in laboratory studies ([Shea and Morgan, 1979](R-shea-1979-contextual)) but, as you will see in [the motor-learning lesson](#w03-l3), with more uncertainty about how far the effects carry into real practice.
How each difficulty works in practice

**Retrieval practice** means pulling information out of memory rather than putting it back in. Low-stakes quizzes, explaining a procedure from memory before checking it, sketching a play diagram from scratch, or answering “what would you do next?” before the answer is shown all qualify. The retrieval must be genuinely effortful: looking at the answer and nodding along is rereading in disguise.

**Spacing** means distributing the same amount of practice over more sessions with gaps between them. The gaps allow some forgetting, which makes the next retrieval harder and more productive. Spacing has an awkward property for organizations: it takes longer on the calendar, even when total practice time is identical, and so it collides with schedules built around intensive courses and boot camps.

**Interleaving** means mixing different kinds of problems or tasks within a session instead of practicing one kind at a time. Its value lies in forcing a choice. When every problem in a block is the same type, the learner never practices deciding which approach applies; in a mixed set, choosing is part of the task. Interleaving is especially relevant when the real challenge is recognizing which situation you are in — a diagnosis, a market condition, an opponent’s tendency.

Why do people resist these methods? Because the feeling of learning comes from fluency — how easily material comes to mind during practice — and fluency is highest under exactly the conditions that produce the least durable learning. Learners in the testing-effect experiments were more confident after restudying, not after testing ([Roediger and Karpicke, 2006](R-roediger-2006-test-enhanced)), and the review of learning versus performance documents the same misreading among learners and instructors across many paradigms ([Soderstrom and Bjork, 2015](R-soderstrom-2015-learning)).

challenge.text: Three limits keep this idea honest. First, a difficulty is desirable only if the learner can eventually succeed. Retrieval that fails completely, with no feedback, may teach nothing; random mixing of tasks a beginner cannot yet perform may produce only confusion. Difficulty is a dose, not a virtue, and the right dose depends on what the learner already knows.

Second, the evidence is uneven across techniques. Retrieval practice and spacing rest on broad bodies of work; interleaving was rated only moderate because its evidence base was narrower ([Dunlosky et al., 2013](R-dunlosky-2013-improving)). A principle that is strong for learning vocabulary or medical facts is not automatically strong for learning a swing, a surgical knot or a negotiation.

Third, organizations do not only want learning. Sometimes they need performance now: a team preparing for tomorrow’s inspection, a player who must compete tonight, a pilot about to take a check ride. In those moments, warm-up repetition that boosts immediate performance may be exactly right. The learning–performance distinction does not tell you to always choose difficulty; it tells you to know which outcome you are buying.

challenge.title: Methodological note: the retention interval is the whole story

blocks.text: Many training evaluations measure outcomes at the end of the session. The testing-effect experiments show why that can mislead: the ranking of conditions reversed between the five-minute test and the delayed tests ([Roediger and Karpicke, 2006](R-roediger-2006-test-enhanced)). When two conditions cross over like this, an immediate test will not merely underestimate the better method; it will pick the wrong winner.

Three design rules follow. Measure after a delay long enough for forgetting to occur, ideally matched to how long the skill must last. Measure in a context that differs from practice (a transfer test), because practice conditions supply cues that real conditions will not. And keep learners’ self-ratings separate from performance measures: confidence is data about the learner’s beliefs, not about their memory. Each rule raises the cost of evaluation, which is one reason most organizations skip them.

apply.text: Consider how the distinction plays out in settings that look nothing alike. A bank’s annual compliance course ends with a quiz taken minutes after the content, and nearly everyone passes; a better design would quiz employees again, briefly, months later, and teach by asking questions first. A law firm onboarding new associates on court deadlines could replace a reading packet with short weekly retrieval exercises spaced across the first quarter. An army unit drilling a procedure could mix scenarios unpredictably instead of rehearsing them in a fixed order. These are hypothetical designs, but each applies a principle with strong evidence for knowledge that must be recalled under pressure.

apply.title: Executive twist: your dashboard rewards the wrong thing

blocks.text: Imagine you run a development department whose quarterly report shows practice-session success rates rising, trainee satisfaction at record highs and every module completed on time. A new staff member proposes redesigning sessions so that success rates will fall and satisfaction will probably drop for a while. You have no long-term data, your budget review is in six weeks, and the people who report to you are proud of the current numbers.

The question is not whether the new design is better — you do not yet know. It is what evidence you would need, and how to buy that evidence cheaply. A defensible move is to run both designs for one cohort, add a delayed retention test and a transfer test that neither group practiced, and tell your own leadership in advance that the new design is expected to look worse during sessions. Pre-registering the expectation protects the experiment from being killed by the very signal it predicts.

apply.text: In player development, the same trap appears in the metrics staff watch daily. Practice data — strike rates in a bullpen session, contact quality in the cage, success on a receiving drill — are performance measures taken in conditions the practice itself controls. Durable learning shows up later and elsewhere: in the first session after a few days off, in a different drill, in a game. A development program that wants to know whether its practice designs work needs scheduled “cold” checks and transfer checks, not only better tracking of what happens inside each session.
Name one training program you have led or attended. What did it measure, and when? What single change to its measurement would have told you whether anyone learned?

retain.text: Performance is what you observe during practice; learning is what remains after a delay and transfers to new conditions. Retrieval practice and spacing have the strongest evidence for durable learning of knowledge; interleaving is promising with a narrower base. Desirable difficulties lower in-session performance and feel worse, so learners, instructors and dashboards systematically prefer the less effective condition. The defense is measurement: delayed tests, transfer tests, and confidence measured separately from competence.
Without looking back: what reversed between the five-minute test and the one-week test in the testing-effect experiments, and what happened to students’ confidence?
Which two techniques received the highest utility rating in the review of ten learning techniques, and which two popular techniques received low ratings?
Explain to a skeptical colleague, in two sentences, why a session with more errors might be the better session.

takeaways: Learning must be inferred from delayed and changed-context tests; in-session performance can mislead in either direction.
Retrieval practice and spacing have the strongest evidence; interleaving is promising but less certain.
Desirable difficulties are desirable only when the learner can eventually succeed.
Learner confidence and instructor impressions tend to favor the less effective practice condition.
Decide whether you need performance now or learning later, and measure accordingly.

check.prompt: A sales team completes a product-knowledge course and scores 94% on a quiz taken at the end of the final session. Which additional result would give you the strongest evidence that the team learned the material?

A different set of questions, given unannounced five weeks later, still produces high scores.
The same quiz, retaken an hour later, produces 97%.
Instructors report that trainees were engaged and made few errors in role-plays.

check.explanation: Learning is a durable change that supports retention and transfer, so it must be measured after a delay and ideally with items that were not practiced. An unannounced test five weeks later with new questions tests both. The other options measure satisfaction, immediate performance or in-session impressions, all of which can be high when little is retained.

lessons.title: Deliberate Practice and Its Critics: What Explains Expertise?
lessons.summary: Deliberate practice describes what high-quality practice looks like, but the claim that accumulated practice explains most differences between people has not held up well.
objectives: Define deliberate practice and distinguish it from play, work, competition and mere repetition.
Interpret “variance explained” correctly and explain why a modest figure does not mean practice is unimportant.
Evaluate both sides of the deliberate-practice debate, including the replication of its founding study.
lessons.executive: Deliberate-practice theory gave organizations a valuable description of high-quality practice: specific goals, effortful work on weaknesses, immediate feedback, expert design. It also produced a popular myth — that roughly ten thousand hours of practice make anyone an expert. The evidence separates the two. Meta-analyses find that accumulated practice explains a real but modest share of performance differences — about 18% in sport, and about 1% among elite athletes — and the founding study replicated with a smaller effect. Its defenders reply that the critics measured the wrong kind of practice. For leaders, the practical conclusion is to invest in practice quality while not treating hours, or a single theory, as a talent strategy.

explore.text: A hypothetical software company launches an internal “mastery academy.” Its pitch deck states that expertise takes ten thousand hours of deliberate practice, so every engineer will log practice hours in a dashboard, and promotion committees will see the totals. A technology consultancy, a regional orchestra and a youth sports federation have adopted similar language. The idea is attractive because it is egalitarian, measurable and actionable: anyone can become excellent, and the path is time.

Before reading on, write down your estimate: across studies of sport, what share of the differences in performance between athletes do you think is explained by differences in how much they have practiced? Then estimate the same share among elite athletes only.

Hold your estimates. This lesson asks two questions that are often blurred together. First, what makes a practice hour valuable? Second, how much of the difference between people — between the good and the great, the starter and the reserve — does accumulated practice explain? Deliberate-practice theory has a strong answer to the first question and a contested answer to the second.

understand.text: The original theory

Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Römer proposed that expert performance results from a long period of **deliberate practice**: effortful activity designed specifically to improve current performance, typically with a teacher who identifies weaknesses and designs tasks to address them, and with immediate feedback and repetition with refinement. They argued that many characteristics once attributed to innate talent are the result of intense practice extended for a minimum of ten years. Their supporting evidence came from music students grouped by skill level, whose retrospective estimates of accumulated practice were higher in the more skilled groups ([Ericsson et al., 1993](R-ericsson-1993-role)).

A surgeon operating on a routine list; a team playing a league match
Planned sessions, often in groups, not individualized
Individualized, effortful, designed by a teacher or expert, immediate feedback, repetition with refinement
A violinist working one bar at a time on a passage her teacher flagged
understand.note: APERTURE synthesis of the definitions used in the cited debate. The boundary between structured and deliberate practice is exactly what the two sides dispute.

understand.text: The definition is demanding. Deliberate practice is not simply “time on task.” It is targeted, usually not inherently enjoyable, and depends on someone who knows what the next improvement should be ([Ericsson et al., 1993](R-ericsson-1993-role)). That is why the theory became so influential among coaches, surgeons and music teachers: it describes good teaching.

blocks.text: When researchers say practice “explains 18% of the variance in performance,” they mean the following. Take a group of people who differ in performance. Some of those differences line up with differences in how much they practiced. The share of the spread in performance that can be predicted from the spread in practice is the variance explained, written R² — for a single predictor, the square of the correlation r. A correlation of about .42 corresponds to roughly 18% of variance explained (.42 × .42 ≈ .18).

Three cautions follow. Variance explained describes differences between people in a particular sample, not how much any individual would improve by practicing more. It depends on how much the sample varies: if everyone practices about the same amount, practice cannot explain differences among them even if it is essential for everyone. And a small R² can still matter a great deal in competitive settings where small differences decide outcomes.

understand.text: What the meta-analyses found

understand.caption: Share of performance differences explained by accumulated deliberate practice, by domain
understand.note: Source: Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald (2014). Professions are plotted at 1 as an upper bound; the paper reports less than 1%.

understand.text: A meta-analysis across domains found that deliberate practice explained about 26% of performance variance in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and less than 1% in professions. The authors concluded that deliberate practice is important but not as important as had been argued ([Macnamara et al., 2014](R-macnamara-2014-deliberate)). A sport-specific meta-analysis reached a similar overall figure — about 18% — and found that among elite athletes, accumulated practice explained only about 1% of performance differences ([Macnamara et al., 2016](R-macnamara-2016-relationship)).

The founding study was also revisited. A replication of the violin study did not reproduce the original core finding that accumulated deliberate practice corresponded to each skill level; the relationship was substantial but considerably smaller than first reported. Participants also rated teacher-designed practice as less relevant to improvement than practice alone, which complicates the original definition ([Macnamara and Maitra, 2019](R-macnamara-2019-role)).

Return to the estimates you wrote at the start of this lesson. The popular account of expertise implies that practice explains most of the differences between athletes and matters most at the top. The meta-analytic answers — under a fifth overall and close to nothing among elite athletes — contradict both implications. If your estimates were well above these figures, the gap is useful: it marks a belief held more strongly than the evidence warrants.
From hours to quality

Both sides of the debate converge on one recommendation: stop measuring practice only by its duration. Ericsson and Harwell urge researchers to record the quality of practice — whether the performer is concentrating, analyzing errors and solving problems — rather than hours alone ([Ericsson and Harwell, 2019](R-ericsson-2019-deliberate)). For an organization, that recommendation is more actionable than any variance estimate.

items: **Target:** Is there a specific, current weakness the session addresses, stated before the session starts?
**Difficulty:** Is the work near the edge of current capability — hard enough to produce errors, not so hard that success is impossible?
**Feedback:** Does the performer find out quickly and accurately how each attempt compares with the target?
**Design:** Has someone with relevant expertise designed or approved the task, rather than defaulting to habit?
**Attention:** Is the performer mentally engaged, or completing repetitions on autopilot?
**Follow-up:** Is progress on the target checked later, after a delay, rather than only within the session?

understand.caption: How a modest correlation became a popular rule

steps.label: Original claim
steps.text: Groups at higher skill levels reported more accumulated deliberate practice, over at least ten years.

steps.label: Simplification
steps.text: A group average is retold as a threshold number of hours.

steps.label: Generalization
steps.text: The number is applied to every domain and every person.

steps.label: Causal leap
steps.text: Practice is assumed to cause the skill difference, rather than skill, enjoyment or support causing more practice.

steps.label: Policy
steps.text: Organizations count hours and treat them as a measure of development.

challenge.text: The two sides of the debate are worth stating at full strength. Ericsson and Harwell argue that the meta-analyses averaged across activities that do not meet the original definition — they call it structured practice — and that when only studies matching the definition are analyzed, practice explains considerably more variance: 29%, and 61% after correcting for measurement error. They urge researchers to measure the quality of practice, such as concentration, analysis and problem solving, not just its duration ([Ericsson and Harwell, 2019](R-ericsson-2019-deliberate)). On the other side stand estimates drawn from all available studies that relate practice to performance, and a direct replication of the founding study that found a smaller effect ([Macnamara et al., 2014](R-macnamara-2014-deliberate); [Macnamara and Maitra, 2019](R-macnamara-2019-role)). APERTURE’s reading: a reanalysis restricted to a small, selected subset of studies, with corrections that depend on uncertain reliability estimates, is a weaker basis for the strong claim than its headline figures suggest — but the critics’ broad definitions may indeed dilute the effect of high-quality practice. The honest summary is that the size of the effect is unresolved.

You do not need to settle this debate to act well. Notice where the two sides agree: the quality of practice matters more than its quantity, and hours alone are a poor measure. They disagree about how much of the difference between people practice can explain, which matters for talent identification and selection more than for practice design.

Two further problems sit under both sides. First, almost all of this evidence is correlational and retrospective: people estimate, years later, how much they practiced. Second, causation can run backward. People who are initially better at something often enjoy it more, receive more coaching and opportunity, and therefore practice more. A correlation between practice and skill is consistent with practice causing skill, skill causing practice, or a third factor causing both.

The sport meta-analysis authors suggest that other factors deserve study — for example, the age at which people start an activity and certain cognitive abilities — while emphasizing that practice still matters ([Macnamara et al., 2016](R-macnamara-2016-relationship)). This is a multifactorial view of expertise: practice is necessary and helpful, but differences in outcome reflect many interacting causes.

challenge.title: Methodological note: range restriction and the elite paradox

blocks.text: Why would practice explain about 18% of differences across all athletes but only about 1% among elite athletes? Part of the answer is statistical. Elite samples are selected: everyone in them has practiced a great deal. When a variable barely varies within a sample, it cannot predict much of the variation in an outcome, even if it was essential for getting into the sample in the first place. The same logic explains why height predicts little about scoring among professional basketball players, although almost all of them are tall.

The implication is subtle. The elite-level result does not show that practice stops mattering at the top. It shows that, among people who have all practiced a lot, differences in accumulated hours are not what separates them. For a decision-maker comparing elite candidates, practice history is weak evidence; for a decision-maker designing a development pathway, practice quality is still central.

apply.text: Translate this into three hypothetical decisions. A hospital deciding whether a surgeon is ready for independent practice should look at observed performance on representative cases, not only at logged case numbers. A consulting firm that promotes on “years of experience” is using a variable that may explain little of the difference between strong and weak consultants. A music conservatory selecting students cannot infer ability from reported practice hours, but it can teach every student to practice more deliberately. In each case the theory helps with design and the critique helps with selection.

blocks.text: Suppose your department proposes a 20% increase in scheduled practice time across all developing performers, funded by cutting individualized coaching. The proposal cites deliberate-practice research. You have no internal data on how practice time relates to development outcomes, and the coaches who would lose individualized time are the most experienced.

A disciplined response distinguishes the two claims. The research cited supports the value of individualized, feedback-rich, effortful practice — which is precisely what the proposal cuts. It does not support the idea that more hours of generic practice reliably produce better outcomes. Before approving, you might ask for a small trial that varies the quality of practice rather than its quantity, with retention and transfer measures, and for a plan to track whether added hours raise injury or burnout risk.

apply.text: In player development, deliberate-practice ideas are most useful as a checklist for session quality: Does each player have a specific, current target? Is the work effortful and near the edge of capability? Is feedback immediate and informative? Has someone with expertise designed the task? They are least useful as a talent theory. A club that treats practice volume as the main driver of development risks overloading players, rewarding attendance over improvement, and misreading individual differences in response to the same program. Logging hours is easy; logging the quality of practice — target, difficulty, feedback, outcome — is harder and far more informative.

Think of a performer you know who practiced more than almost anyone and plateaued, and one who practiced less and improved fast. What, other than hours, differed between them? Which of those differences could an organization influence?

retain.text: Deliberate practice is effortful, individualized practice designed to improve specific weaknesses with immediate feedback. Its description of practice quality remains useful. Its stronger claim — that accumulated deliberate practice explains most differences in expertise — is not well supported: meta-analyses find modest shares of variance explained, about 18% in sport and about 1% among elite athletes, and the founding study replicated with a smaller effect. Defenders argue the critics measured the wrong kind of practice. Both sides agree that quality beats quantity.

State the strongest argument Ericsson and Harwell make against the meta-analyses, and the strongest response to it.

takeaways: Deliberate practice is defined by quality — targeted, effortful, expert-designed, feedback-rich — not by hours.
Accumulated practice explains a real but modest share of performance differences, and very little among elite performers.
Variance explained describes differences between people in a sample, not how much one person can improve.
The founding study replicated with a smaller effect; the debate over definitions is unresolved.
Use the theory to design practice; do not use practice hours as a talent measure.

check.prompt: A meta-analysis finds that among elite athletes, accumulated practice explains about 1% of the variance in performance. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Practice does not matter for elite athletes, so elite programs can safely reduce training.
Among athletes who have all practiced a great deal, differences in accumulated hours do little to distinguish better from worse performers.
Elite performance is determined by genetics.
The meta-analysis must be flawed, because practice obviously matters.

check.explanation: Variance explained describes differences between people in a sample. Elite samples are selected for high practice, so practice varies little among them and cannot predict much of their variation in performance. This says nothing about whether practice was necessary to reach that level, and nothing about the specific causes of the remaining variance.

lessons.title: Motor Learning: Practice Schedules, Feedback, Attention — and a Live Debate
lessons.summary: Motor-learning research offers powerful laboratory findings on practice scheduling, feedback and attention, but several of them shrink in applied settings or under bias correction, and the field’s two main theoretical camps still disagree about what is being learned.
objectives: Explain contextual interference, practice variability, feedback frequency and attentional focus, and what each predicts for acquisition, retention and transfer.
Grade each motor-learning principle by the strength of its laboratory, applied and bias-corrected evidence.
Compare information-processing and ecological-dynamics accounts of skill learning and state what each implies for practice design.
lessons.executive: Coaches in every movement-based field — surgery, aviation, music, the military, sport — now hear the same prescriptions: randomize practice, give less feedback, cue attention outward, design representative tasks. Each has a real research base and a real weakness. Random practice reliably beats blocked practice for retention in laboratory tasks, but the benefit is smaller and uncertain in applied settings. The external-focus advantage looks large in a 2021 meta-analysis and close to zero after a 2024 bias-corrected reanalysis. Theory is divided between information-processing and ecological-dynamics camps. Leaders should treat these principles as sensible defaults to test, not as settled science to mandate.

explore.text: A surgical residency program teaches interns three suturing techniques in its skills lab. One instructor runs blocked practice: twenty repetitions of the first technique, then twenty of the second, then twenty of the third, with a comment after nearly every stitch. Another runs mixed practice: the three techniques in an unpredictable order, with a brief summary of feedback after every few stitches. By the end of the afternoon, the first group’s stitches look markedly better, and its interns leave confident. The program is hypothetical; the question it poses is real.

Predict: which group performs better at the end of the session? Which performs better when tested, without warm-up, ten days later? Which performs better on a fourth suturing pattern neither group practiced? Rate your confidence in each answer from 50% to 100%.

Shea and Morgan ran the laboratory version of this experiment. Participants learned three movement patterns, knocking down barriers in set sequences, either in blocks or in a random order. Blocked practice produced better performance during acquisition. Random practice produced better retention — particularly when retention was tested in a random order — and better transfer, especially to the most complex transfer task ([Shea and Morgan, 1979](R-shea-1979-contextual)). The schedule that looked worse taught more. This became known as the **contextual interference effect**.

blocks.text: Motor-learning experiments have three phases. In **acquisition**, learners practice under the conditions being compared — blocked or random, frequent or reduced feedback. In a **retention** test, after a delay, everyone performs the practiced skill under the same conditions, usually without feedback. In a **transfer** test, everyone performs a variation of the skill or the same skill in a new context. Only retention and transfer tell you about learning. An experiment, or a coaching evaluation, that stops at the end of acquisition measures performance alone.

understand.text: Practice schedules: blocked, serial and random

Blocked practice repeats one task before moving to the next; serial practice cycles through tasks in a fixed order; random practice mixes them unpredictably. In the laboratory, random practice tends to depress acquisition performance and improve retention and transfer ([Shea and Morgan, 1979](R-shea-1979-contextual)). A 2024 meta-analysis of 34 studies found that high contextual interference improved transfer on average, with a medium overall effect (SMD = 0.55) and a larger effect in laboratory studies (SMD = 0.75) ([Czyż et al., 2024](R-czyz-2024-effect)).

Two classic explanations compete, and both are hypotheses about mechanism rather than established facts. The *reconstruction* account holds that switching tasks forces the learner to partially forget and then rebuild the movement plan on each attempt, and the rebuilding strengthens it. The *elaboration* account holds that having several tasks in working memory at once invites comparison, so the learner understands what distinguishes them. Both predict that difficulty during practice is part of what produces learning.
Practice variability

A related idea concerns variation within a single skill: throwing to different distances, putting from different spots, landing in different crosswinds. Information-processing theories propose that learners build a general rule linking movement parameters to outcomes, and that varied practice builds a better rule than constant practice. Ecological approaches reach a similar prescription for a different reason: variation teaches the learner to adapt to the conditions of performance. This course’s sources do not include a current meta-analysis of variability of practice, so treat the principle as plausible and widely used, with its size uncertain.
Feedback: how much, what kind, and when

Learners always receive intrinsic feedback — what they see and feel. Coaches add augmented feedback: **knowledge of results** (the outcome, such as where the ball landed or the time recorded) and **knowledge of performance** (the movement pattern, such as the elbow angle or the hand position). Augmented feedback can be given after every attempt, faded as the learner improves, summarized after several attempts, or provided when the learner asks.

The **guidance hypothesis** proposes that frequent augmented feedback improves performance during practice but can impair retention, because learners come to depend on it instead of on their own error detection. Reduced or faded feedback is one of the manipulations Soderstrom and Bjork review as moving performance and learning in different directions ([Soderstrom and Bjork, 2015](R-soderstrom-2015-learning)). The applied evidence is less clear than the laboratory demonstrations, and the right frequency very likely depends on the learner’s stage and the complexity of the skill.

A broader warning comes from outside motor learning. A large meta-analysis of feedback interventions in many settings found a positive average effect but highly variable results, with a substantial share of interventions lowering performance; feedback that drew attention to the self rather than to the task tended to do worse ([Kluger and DeNisi, 1996](R-kluger-1996-effects)). The volume and focus of feedback are design choices, not free goods. (This record could not be re-verified in this edition; see the library note.)
Attentional focus

An **internal focus** directs attention to body movements (“extend your elbow”); an **external focus** directs it to the movement’s effect (“send the ball toward the far post”). A 2021 set of meta-analyses pooled 73 studies for performance and 40 for learning and reported advantages for an external focus: Hedges’ g of about 0.26 for performance and about 0.58 for both retention and transfer, without significant moderation by age, health or skill level ([Chua et al., 2021](R-chua-2021-superiority)). Read the next section before relying on those numbers.

understand.text: Two ways to explain skill

Underneath the prescriptions sits a theoretical disagreement. **Information-processing** accounts treat the learner as a system that perceives, decides and executes, storing generalized motor programs and rules that practice refines. **Ecological dynamics** treats skill as an adaptive relationship between a performer and an environment: the performer learns to perceive opportunities for action and to coordinate movement under changing constraints. Its coaching method, the **constraints-led approach**, manipulates constraints of the individual, the task and the environment — field size, equipment, rules, opponents — so that effective movement solutions emerge, rather than prescribing a single technical model.

challenge.text: The contextual interference effect is the clearest example of a laboratory finding whose applied size is disputed. The 2024 transfer meta-analysis that found a medium overall effect also found that in applied settings the effect was small and not statistically significant (SMD = 0.34), and in young participants it was negligible (SMD = 0.12) ([Czyż et al., 2024](R-czyz-2024-effect)). A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of sport practice went further, finding little evidence that the benefit generalizes to applied physical-education and sport settings and calling it a myth ([Ammar et al., 2023](R-ammar-2023-myth)). The two research groups have since exchanged published critiques. The defensible position is that mixing practice is a reasonable default for learners who already have a stable basic pattern, not a law.

Attentional focus is a second live dispute. The 2021 meta-analyses reported medium-sized learning benefits for an external focus ([Chua et al., 2021](R-chua-2021-superiority)). A 2024 reanalysis of the same literature using robust Bayesian methods found moderate to strong evidence of publication bias in every analysis; after correction, estimates fell to about g = 0.01 for performance, 0.15 for retention and 0.09 for transfer, and Bayes factors favored no effect ([McKay et al., 2024](R-mckay-2024-reporting)). Bias-correction methods rest on their own assumptions, so this does not prove that external cues never help. It does mean the principle cannot be presented as established.

A third limit concerns the learner. A plausible and widely used idea — often called the challenge point — holds that the most useful level of difficulty depends on the learner’s skill: a beginner may be overwhelmed by random practice that would help an experienced performer. The negligible effect of contextual interference in young participants is consistent with this, though it does not prove it ([Czyż et al., 2024](R-czyz-2024-effect)). Treat difficulty as something to calibrate to each learner, not to maximize.

Finally, the theoretical debate is not settled by either side’s rhetoric. Few studies compare a full constraints-led program with a well-designed traditional program on retention and transfer in real competition. Many claims on both sides are theoretical. An executive should notice when a coaching philosophy is defended mainly by appeal to its own theory, and ask what outcome data would change the proponent’s mind.

challenge.title: Methodological note: “motor engrams” — a useful word, a weak explanation

blocks.text: Coaches often say a drill is “building the engram” or “grooving the pattern.” The word engram comes from memory research and refers to the physical trace of a memory in the nervous system. Neuroscience has made real progress in identifying the cells and circuits that participate in specific memories, mostly in animal studies of relatively simple learning. That work is fascinating, but it does not tell a coach which drill to run.

The problem is not that engrams are unreal; it is that the claim is unfalsifiable at the level of a practice session. No coach can observe an engram forming. Any drill can be said to build one, and any failure can be blamed on an engram not yet consolidated. The engram language therefore adds confidence without adding evidence. The testable questions remain behavioral: after a delay, without the coach, in a new context, can the performer do it? Treat neuroscience vocabulary in coaching materials as a cue to ask for retention and transfer data.

apply.text: Apply the grading across fields, using hypothetical programs. A flight-training department could vary simulator scenarios so that pilots cannot predict which failure comes next, while recording performance on a later unannounced check rather than in the session. A conservatory teacher could have a student rotate among three difficult passages instead of perfecting one before moving on, once each passage can be played slowly. A military marksmanship program could vary positions, distances and time pressure, using outcome feedback summarized after each string of shots rather than technique comments after every round. A surgical skills lab could fade instructor comments over a curriculum and test each technique four weeks later. In each case the design follows a reasonable default and builds in the measurement that would show whether it worked.

For player development, take a receiving or blocking progression for catchers as an illustration. A common design uses a pitching machine set to one location and speed, repeated in blocks, with technique comments after most reps: high in-session success, constant conditions, internal cues and heavy guidance. A redesign might begin with blocked work only until the basic pattern is stable, then mix pitch types and locations from live arms, give outcome-based feedback summarized after short sets, and use cues about the target or the ball rather than about body parts. Neither design is proven superior for a given player. The professional step is to state which elements are evidence-based defaults, which are hypotheses, and to add a weekly cold check that shows whether the change improved anything that lasts.

retain.text: Random practice, varied practice, reduced feedback and external cues all aim to trade in-session performance for retention and transfer. Laboratory evidence for contextual interference is consistent, but applied effects are small and disputed. The external-focus advantage is contested after bias correction. Information-processing and ecological-dynamics accounts disagree about what is learned and how much coaches should instruct; head-to-head evidence is thin. Calibrate difficulty to the learner, use principles as defaults to test, and judge them by retention and transfer.

lessons.title: Expertise, Transfer and the Coach’s Job: Cognitive Load, Myths and Measurement
lessons.summary: Experts differ from novices in what they have stored, skills transfer less widely than people hope, learning styles are not a sound basis for instruction, and a development system is only as good as its measures of learning.
objectives: Explain cognitive load and the expertise reversal effect, and apply them to how coaches explain and demonstrate.
Distinguish near from far transfer and judge claims that a training activity builds a general capacity.
Explain why the learning-styles matching hypothesis lacks support and which individual differences should shape instruction instead.
Design a measurement plan that separates learning from performance.
lessons.executive: Leaders buy and run development systems built on claims about how people learn. Some claims are well supported: working memory is limited, so instruction that overloads it fails, and the best method depends on the learner’s current expertise. Some are weak: skills rarely transfer to distant domains, and matching instruction to a learner’s preferred “style” has not been shown to help. The executive task is to grade claims before funding them, to individualize by what learners know and can do rather than by labels, and to insist on measures of retention and transfer. A development system that cannot show what lasts is a system for producing good-looking practice.

explore.text: A hypothetical consulting firm begins onboarding with a questionnaire that classifies each new analyst as a visual, auditory or kinesthetic learner. Materials are tailored: diagrams for the visual group, recorded explanations for the auditory group, hands-on workshops for the kinesthetic group. Satisfaction scores are excellent, and the head of learning cites them when the budget is reviewed. Across town, a hospital simulation center tailors training differently: novices work through detailed worked cases, while experienced clinicians go straight to unscripted scenarios.

Before reading on: what result would show that matching materials to learning styles improves learning? Would the consulting firm’s satisfaction scores count? What would the hospital need to show to justify its approach?

Both organizations individualize. One individualizes by a label learners assign themselves; the other by what learners already know. This lesson argues that the second is supported by research and the first is not — and that the difference matters for how you build a development system, train coaches and evaluate vendors.

understand.title: Prerequisite: working memory and long-term memory

blocks.text: Working memory is where you consciously process information right now; it can handle only a few new elements at a time and loses them within seconds unless they are rehearsed. Long-term memory is effectively unlimited and stores organized knowledge — sometimes called schemas — that lets you treat many elements as one. A chess master sees a familiar position as a single pattern; a novice sees many separate pieces. Much of what we call expertise is a large library of such patterns, available instantly.

understand.text: Cognitive load and what experts have that novices lack

Cognitive load theory builds instruction on that architecture. New information must pass through a limited working memory; organized knowledge in long-term memory effectively expands what the learner can handle. Instruction should manage the load inherent in the material and minimize load created by poor presentation — redundant information, split attention between sources, unnecessary search. One of the theory’s most practical findings is the **expertise reversal effect**: methods that help novices, such as fully worked examples and detailed guidance, can become redundant or harmful for learners who already have the relevant knowledge ([Sweller et al., 2019](R-sweller-2019-cognitive)).

For a coach, the translation is direct. A novice given five technical points after a repetition can process perhaps one; the rest is noise that competes for the same limited capacity. An experienced performer may be slowed by step-by-step instruction that a novice needs. The right amount of instruction is a property of the learner–task pair, not of the coach’s philosophy.

items: **One point at a time.** Give the single most important cue, then let the learner try; stack cues only once the first is automatic.
**Show before you tell.** For movement, a demonstration or a short clip often carries in one look what a paragraph cannot.
**Remove the redundant.** Do not narrate what the learner can already see, and do not present the same information in two places at once.
**Fade guidance as knowledge grows.** Detailed scaffolding for beginners; questions and open problems for experienced performers.
**Check understanding by retrieval.** Ask the learner to state the cue or the plan back, from memory, before the next attempt.

understand.text: Expertise also changes what a learner perceives. Because experts hold organized patterns in long-term memory, they notice meaningful cues — a defender’s shift, an abnormal vital sign, an inconsistency in a contract — that novices overlook, and they see them quickly enough to act. This is why experts are often poor teachers of novices: the steps they no longer notice are exactly the ones the novice needs made explicit. It is also why perceptual and decision skills deserve practice in their own right, in conditions that present the same cues the real task does.
Transfer: near, far and rare

**Transfer** is the use of learning in a context different from the one in which it was acquired. Near transfer — to a similar task or setting — is common. Far transfer — to a substantially different domain — is the hope behind many training products. A review of meta-analyses on chess instruction, music training and working-memory training concluded that far transfer to general cognitive or academic abilities is rare, and that apparent effects shrink as study quality improves ([Sala and Gobet, 2017](R-sala-2017-does)). Even within motor learning, the transfer advantages of a well-studied practice method were smaller and uncertain in applied settings compared with the laboratory ([Czyż et al., 2024](R-czyz-2024-effect)).

understand.text: Learning styles: a testable idea that failed its test

The learning-styles idea holds that people learn best when instruction matches their preferred modality. Pashler and colleagues specified the evidence needed to support it: classify learners by style, randomly assign each group to matched or mismatched instruction, and give everyone the same test. Matching is supported only if the results cross over — each group does best with its own style of instruction. They found that well-designed tests of this kind were virtually absent, that the few that existed did not support the claim, and that the evidence did not justify spending resources on style assessment and matched instruction ([Pashler et al., 2008](R-pashler-2008-learning)).

understand.text: Two points prevent overcorrection. People genuinely have preferences, and some content is better taught in a particular modality for everyone — a movement pattern is easier to show than to describe, a statistical relationship is easier to see in a chart. That is matching instruction to the content, not to the learner’s label. And individual differences in learning are real; they simply are not well captured by sensory styles.
Individual differences that should shape instruction

Which differences should a development system use? The best supported is prior knowledge and skill, because the effectiveness of instructional methods depends on it ([Sweller et al., 2019](R-sweller-2019-cognitive)). Practice history matters, but in sport it explains a minority of performance differences, which points to other contributors that researchers are still investigating ([Macnamara et al., 2016](R-macnamara-2016-relationship)). Motivation, physical characteristics, injury history and life circumstances also differ widely. A sound system individualizes by measured stage and need, not by a questionnaire label.

challenge.text: Cognitive load theory has limits of its own. Load is difficult to measure directly, and much of the research relies on self-rated mental effort; most studies concern academic and technical material rather than motor skills ([Sweller et al., 2019](R-sweller-2019-cognitive)). Applying it to a coach’s instruction during practice is reasonable by analogy — keep instructions few and relevant, adjust guidance to expertise — but it is an extrapolation that a program should test rather than assume.

There is also a tension between this lesson and the previous ones. Cognitive load theory recommends reducing unnecessary difficulty; the desirable-difficulties literature recommends adding certain kinds of difficulty. The two are compatible once you separate the sources. Extraneous load — confusing explanations, too many cues, poorly designed materials — should be cut. Productive difficulty — retrieving instead of rereading, mixing tasks once basics are stable, fading guidance — can be added, in doses calibrated to the learner. A coach who overloads a novice with mixed tasks and ten cues is creating the wrong kind of difficulty.

Finally, coaching rarely operates where evidence is complete. Most practice-design decisions combine some research, a great deal of craft knowledge and local constraints. “Evidence-informed” is a more honest description than “evidence-based” for most of what a development department does. The discipline lies in labelling each element by its support — supported, contested, hypothesis, not supported — and in designing the program so that its hypotheses are tested over time, rather than defended.

challenge.title: Methodological note: why satisfaction data cannot test matching

blocks.text: The matching hypothesis is a claim about an interaction: the effect of the instruction type depends on the learner type. Testing it requires random assignment to matched and mismatched instruction and a common outcome measure ([Pashler et al., 2008](R-pashler-2008-learning)). The consulting firm in this lesson’s opening assigned no one to mismatched materials, so it cannot observe the comparison that matters.

Its satisfaction data add a second problem: learners may simply prefer whatever feels fluent, and fluency is a poor guide to learning. A design with only matched groups and satisfaction outcomes could look successful even if matching harmed learning. When you evaluate any personalization claim — in training, education technology or player development — ask whether anyone was assigned to the non-personalized condition and what outcome was measured, when.

A vendor proposes a three-year contract for a development platform. Its materials claim that the system profiles each learner’s style, builds “motor engrams” through high-repetition drills, guarantees mastery at ten thousand logged hours, uses spaced retrieval for knowledge content, and includes delayed retention testing. Your staff are enthusiastic, the price is significant, and a competitor organization has already signed.

blocks.text: The ledger changes the negotiation. You might accept the supported components, ask the vendor to disable or drop the unsupported ones, and tie renewal to retention and transfer data from your own pilot. The competitor’s decision is not evidence.

apply.text: Similar ledgers apply elsewhere. A hospital simulation center can stage training by expertise — worked cases and detailed debriefs for residents early in training, unscripted scenarios for experienced teams — and check retention months later. A government agency rolling out a new case-management procedure can expect near transfer from realistic practice and little from generic “critical thinking” modules. A military unit can teach new procedures with minimal, focused instruction and measure them in unannounced exercises. These are hypothetical applications of the principles above.

A player development framework built on this lesson would individualize by measured stage rather than by labels; train coaches to give fewer, more relevant cues and to adjust guidance as players progress; label each practice element by its evidence status; and run a measurement calendar with retention checks and transfer checks alongside game data. It would also be candid with staff and players that some of its elements are hypotheses under test. That candor is not weakness; it is what lets the system improve instead of merely persisting.
List three beliefs about learning that are common in your field. Place each in the ledger — supported, contested, hypothesis or not supported — and write the one piece of evidence that would move it.

retain.text: Working memory is limited and expertise is stored knowledge, so the right amount of instruction depends on the learner’s current expertise. Far transfer is rare; expect skills to transfer only where demands overlap. The learning-styles matching hypothesis lacks the crossover evidence it requires; individualize by prior knowledge, skill and need instead. Separate extraneous load, which should be cut, from productive difficulty, which can be added in calibrated doses. Measure retention and transfer, and keep confidence and satisfaction in their place.
What is the expertise reversal effect, and what does it imply for coaching a novice versus a veteran?
Describe the experiment needed to support the learning-styles matching hypothesis. Why can’t satisfaction data substitute for it?
Name two measures of learning and two measures of performance that a development system could collect every month.

takeaways: Instruction must fit working-memory limits; the best method depends on the learner’s expertise.
Near transfer is common; far transfer is rare and should be tested, not assumed.
Matching instruction to learning styles lacks supporting evidence; individualize by knowledge, skill and need.
Cut extraneous load; add productive difficulty in calibrated doses.
Grade every claim in a development system and measure retention and transfer.

check.prompt: An experienced performer finds a highly scripted, step-by-step training module slower and less useful than open practice, while novices find the same module very helpful. Which concept best explains this pattern?

options.text: The learning-styles matching hypothesis
The expertise reversal effect
Range restriction
Far transfer

check.explanation: The expertise reversal effect describes instructional methods that help novices becoming redundant or harmful for learners who already hold the relevant knowledge. Guidance that reduces load for a novice adds unnecessary processing for an expert.

optionFeedback.a: Learning styles concern sensory preferences, not differences in prior knowledge; the matching hypothesis also lacks supporting evidence.
optionFeedback.c: Range restriction is a statistical issue in correlational samples, not an explanation of how instruction interacts with expertise.
optionFeedback.d: Far transfer concerns applying learning in distant domains, not the fit between instruction and expertise.

check.prompt: Which study design could provide evidence for the learning-styles matching hypothesis?

options.text: Survey learners about their preferred style and correlate it with their grades.
Teach every learner in their preferred style and measure satisfaction.
Classify learners by style, randomly assign each to matched or mismatched instruction, give everyone the same test, and look for a crossover.
Compare the average performance of visual and verbal learners on a single test.

check.explanation: The hypothesis predicts an interaction: each type of learner does best with matched instruction. Only random assignment to matched and mismatched instruction, with a common test, can reveal that crossover.

optionFeedback.a: A correlation between preference and grades says nothing about whether matching instruction changes learning.
optionFeedback.b: Without a mismatched comparison group, satisfaction cannot show that matching improved learning.
optionFeedback.d: A difference between groups on one test could reflect many factors and does not test matching at all.
