glossary.definition: A relatively permanent change in capability that supports retention and transfer; it must be inferred from delayed or changed-context tests.
What a learner does during or immediately after practice; an observable but potentially misleading index of learning.
A condition that slows or complicates acquisition but improves long-term retention or transfer, provided the learner can eventually succeed.
Practicing by recalling information or a procedure from memory rather than reviewing it; the basis of the testing effect.
Distributing a fixed amount of practice across separated sessions rather than massing it into one.
Mixing different kinds of problems or tasks within a session so that the learner must choose the approach, not only execute it.
A test of a practiced skill or knowledge after a delay, usually without feedback, used to infer learning.
Effortful, individualized practice designed, often by a teacher, to improve a specific aspect of performance, with immediate feedback and repetition with refinement.
The share of the differences in an outcome across a sample that can be predicted from a variable; for one predictor, the square of the correlation.
Reduced variation in a variable within a selected sample, which weakens its observed relationship with outcomes even if it matters.
The effect in which practicing several tasks in a mixed or random order depresses practice performance but can improve retention and transfer relative to blocked practice.

glossary.term: Knowledge of results and of performance
glossary.definition: Augmented feedback about the outcome of a movement (results) or about the movement pattern itself (performance).
The proposal that frequent augmented feedback aids practice performance but can impair retention by creating dependence on the feedback.
Where a performer directs attention: internally to body movements or externally to the movement’s effect; the claimed external-focus advantage is contested.
An ecological-dynamics coaching method that manipulates individual, task and environmental constraints so that effective movement solutions emerge.
The demand that a task and its presentation place on limited working memory; instruction should reduce load created by poor presentation.
The finding that instructional methods that help novices, such as detailed guidance, can become redundant or harmful for more expert learners.
Use of learning in a similar task or context (near) versus a substantially different domain (far); far transfer is rare.
The claim that instruction matched to a learner’s preferred modality improves learning; it lacks the crossover evidence needed to support it.

exercise.title: Learning Architect

intro.text: You will design a twelve-week practice plan for one skill — a tennis second serve that must land reliably under match pressure — and then redesign it for a different learner. For each plan you choose one option on seven dimensions: who the learner is, the practice schedule, how practice is spread across the week, feedback, practice conditions, retention and transfer checks, and the main attentional cue. The studio totals each option’s effects on six indicators and shows warnings that fire only for particular combinations.

items: Build the plan you would actually run first, without optimizing for the indicators. Note what you chose and why.
Then build two contrasting plans: one that maximizes performance during practice sessions, and one that maximizes retention and transfer. Compare the indicators side by side.
Switch the learner from the novice to the experienced player and keep everything else fixed. Read which warnings appear and disappear.
Open “Show the rules” before you finish. Every effect has a stated rationale and a source, and several are deliberately small because the evidence is contested.

intro.text: Notice in particular the indicator called **What you will know about real learning**. A plan can score well on everything a coach sees and still leave you blind to whether anything lasted. That blindness is a design choice, not a fact of nature.

brief.text: The skill: a second serve in tennis. A good second serve must land in the service box with enough spin and placement that the returner cannot attack it, under the pressure of a tight score. The coach has three hours of court time per week for serve work over twelve weeks. All learners are fictional.

brief.caption: The three fictional learners
rows: Eighteen months of competitive play; the basic serve motion is still unstable
Build a reliable second-serve motion she can repeat
Reliable motion; placement and spin vary under pressure
Turn a reliable motion into a dependable weapon in matches
National-level player; second serve breaks down in tight matches
Keep the serve intact under scoreboard pressure
brief.note: Fictional learners for a teaching exercise.

indicators.label: Retention after two weeks without serve practice
What you will know about real learning

dimensions.label: Learner
dimensions.help: Choose who you are planning for. The learner does not move the indicators directly; it changes which combinations help or hurt (see the warnings).

options.label: Ana, 14 — basic serve motion still unstable
options.why: Learner stage changes how much difficulty is desirable. In a 2024 meta-analysis the transfer benefit of high contextual interference was negligible in young participants.

options.label: Leo, 17 — reliable motion, inconsistent under pressure
options.why: A learner with a stable pattern is the classic candidate for added variability and mixing; difficulty can rise as the motion holds.

options.label: Tomás, 23 — national-level, breaks down in tight matches
options.why: For an experienced performer the problem is usually adaptation to real conditions, not the basic pattern; guidance that helps novices may be redundant.

dimensions.label: Practice schedule across serve types and targets
dimensions.help: How kick, slice and flat second serves are ordered within each session.

options.label: Blocked: 25 kick serves to one target, then 25 slice serves
options.why: Blocked repetition raises in-session success and confidence. In laboratory studies it produced poorer retention and transfer than random practice; applied differences are smaller.

options.label: Serial: a fixed rotation of kick, slice, flat to rotating targets
options.why: An intermediate level of interference; the predictable order keeps performance fairly high.

options.label: Random: the coach calls serve type and target before each serve
options.why: Lower practice performance and confidence. Better retention and transfer in laboratory work, but the applied transfer effect was small and not statistically significant and one meta-analysis calls the applied benefit a myth — so the benefit is set at +1, not +3.

options.label: Progressive: blocked until the motion holds, then increasingly random
options.why: A practitioner compromise consistent with calibrating difficulty to the learner. It is a hypothesis, not a tested prescription, and it depends on the coach judging when to advance.

dimensions.label: Distribution of the same three hours per week
dimensions.help: Total practice time is identical; only its distribution changes.

options.label: One three-hour block on Saturday
options.why: Massing keeps performance high within the block, but distributed practice has stronger evidence for durable retention; fatigue late in a long block also degrades practice quality.

options.label: Two 90-minute sessions
options.why: Moderate spacing: some benefit for retention with little extra scheduling.

options.label: Four 45-minute sessions on different days
options.why: Distributed practice is rated high utility for knowledge and reviewed as a desirable difficulty in motor learning; it costs more scheduling and court bookings.

dimensions.label: Augmented feedback from the coach
dimensions.help: Frequency and kind of information the coach adds to what the learner sees and feels.

options.label: A technique comment after every serve
options.why: Frequent guidance boosts in-session performance; the guidance hypothesis predicts dependence on the coach and weaker retention. Feedback that shifts attention to the self can lower performance.

options.label: Outcome feedback after most serves early, fading to occasional
options.why: Fading keeps early support and builds the learner’s own error detection; the benefit of reduced feedback is clearer in laboratory work than in applied settings.

options.label: Summary after each set of five: placement chart plus one cue
options.why: Summary feedback limits guidance and keeps attention on outcomes, at the cost of slower correction within the session.

options.label: The learner asks for feedback when wanted
options.why: Supports autonomy and may help engagement. This course has not verified current evidence on learning benefits of learner-controlled feedback, so no retention effect is assumed.

dimensions.label: Practice conditions
dimensions.help: How much the conditions of practice resemble and vary like those of matches.

options.label: Same court, same target, no returner
options.why: Stable conditions maximize clean repetitions and in-session success but rehearse little of what changes in matches.

options.label: Varied targets, both sides of the court, different balls and wind
options.why: Variation within a skill is a widely used default supported in classic studies; this course has not verified a current meta-analysis, so the effects are set modestly.

options.label: Representative: serves in scored points against a live returner
options.why: Preserves the perception–action demands of competition, which ecological-dynamics approaches emphasize. Transfer is plausibly highest, but head-to-head trials are scarce and live returners cost time.

dimensions.label: Retention and transfer checks
dimensions.help: What, if anything, you measure outside ordinary practice.

options.label: None — judge progress from practice sessions
options.why: Cheapest, but you will only ever see performance, the measure most easily inflated by practice design.

options.label: Weekly cold check: 20 second serves to targets before any warm-up drills, logged
options.why: Measures retention after days without serve practice. Retrieving the skill cold may itself help; retrieval benefits are well established for knowledge and less studied for motor skills.

options.label: Weekly cold checks plus a monthly match-play test against an unfamiliar returner
options.why: Shows both retention and transfer. Costs scheduling time and makes progress look slower, which tests the patience of staff and learner.

dimensions.label: Main attentional cue
dimensions.help: The one instruction the coach repeats most often.

options.label: Internal: “snap the wrist and keep the elbow high”
options.why: Directs attention to body movements. A 2021 meta-analysis favored external cues, but a 2024 bias-corrected reanalysis found effects near zero, so the penalty is small.

options.label: External: “brush up the back of the ball toward the net post”
options.why: Directs attention to the effect on the ball. Contested: medium effects in 2021, near zero after 2024 bias correction. Cheap to use; do not oversell.

options.label: Analogy: “throw the racket head up at the sky”
options.why: An analogy packs a whole movement into one image and may reduce explicit load; this course has not verified evidence on analogy learning, so no effect is assumed.

rules.text: Overload risk. Ana does not yet have a stable serve motion. Calling a different serve on every attempt asks her to switch among three serves she cannot yet perform reliably — more likely an undesirable difficulty than a desirable one. The 2024 transfer meta-analysis found a negligible effect in young participants. Consider the progressive schedule.

Illusion risk. Tomás will look excellent in blocked sessions, because he can already groove one serve at a time. The sessions will tell you almost nothing about the problem you were asked to solve, which appears only under match pressure.

Overload and dependence. A body-focused technique comment after every serve adds explicit information on every attempt. Expect strong session numbers, dependence on the coach and limited retention. One cue at a time is the safer default.

You are paying the confidence cost of random practice without collecting the evidence that would show its benefit. Staff and learner will see worse sessions and nothing else. This is how promising designs get abandoned.
Self-sealing plan. The only evidence you collect — practice performance — is the measure this plan inflates most. Every report will look good, whether or not anything lasts.

Live points for a beginner offer high transfer potential and a high failure rate. Rather than removing the returner, scale the constraints — a cooperative returner, a larger target area, modified scoring — so that success is possible.

Coherent plan for Tomás. Practice conditions resemble the problem, and the checks will show whether improvement transfers. Session numbers will look worse; agree with the player and staff in advance that this is expected.

Useful tension. With one weekly block, the cold check comes after six days without serve practice and will expose forgetting honestly. If cold-check numbers stay flat while Saturday numbers rise, you are looking at the learning–performance gap in your own data.

Well-matched progression for Leo: difficulty and guidance both move with skill. The risk sits in the judgment calls — when to advance and when to fade — so write the criteria down before the program starts.

config.disclaimer: Effects are ordinal teaching heuristics drawn from the cited research, not predictions. Several principles are contested or uncertain in applied settings, so their effects are deliberately small and explained in each option’s rationale.

debrief.text: If you built a performance-maximizing plan and a learning-maximizing plan, you probably saw the indicators pull in opposite directions: blocked, massed, constant practice with frequent technique comments scores well on session performance and confidence, and poorly on retention, transfer and visibility. The learning-oriented plan reverses the pattern and costs more coach time. That trade-off is the learning–performance distinction expressed as a budget.

Switching the learner should have changed the warnings more than the totals. The same random schedule that is a reasonable default for an experienced player can overload a beginner, and the same live-point practice that suits a national-level player needs scaled constraints for a novice. Good practice design is conditional on the learner; a single program for everyone is rarely optimal.

What the exercise does **not** show: the size of any effect for a real learner. The numbers are ordinal and deliberately conservative where the evidence is contested — contextual interference in applied settings, attentional focus after bias correction, learner-controlled feedback. They encode a direction and a level of confidence, not a forecast. The one effect that is not uncertain is the visibility indicator: if you do not test retention and transfer, you will not know, whichever plan you choose.

assumptions: All learners, sessions and numbers are fictional; effects are ordinal heuristics on a −3 to +3 scale per option, totaled and clamped to −6…+6.
Total practice time is held constant at three hours per week across all plans.
Effects of contested principles (random practice in applied settings, attentional focus, learner-controlled feedback) are set small or at zero to reflect uncertainty.
Learner stage changes outcomes only through the warnings, not through direct effects.
Coach cost includes planning and court time, not the value of the coach’s alternative uses of time.

case.title: The Development Dilemma
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. Varnholt Medical Center and its residency program are invented; numbers are synthetic and chosen for teaching.

body.text: Dr. Lena Abara had two weeks and one meeting. The chair of surgery at Varnholt Medical Center, Dr. Ines Okafor, wanted a recommendation on whether the general surgery residency should replace the way it had trained new interns in technical skills for more than two decades. “Not a literature review,” Okafor had said. “A recommendation, what it costs, and what we do if it doesn’t work.”

Abara had directed the residency for two years. Its forty residents, eight per year, were well regarded; graduates passed their board examinations at rates the department was proud of, and the program had no history of serious accreditation findings. That record was part of the problem. Any change would be measured against a system that, by most visible signs, worked.
The Varnholt model

The established process was known internally as the Varnholt model, and it had been built largely by Dr. Walter Pruitt, the vice chair, who had operated at Varnholt for twenty-six years. Each July, new interns attended a two-day skills “boot camp”: stations for knot tying, suturing, laparoscopic instrument handling and stapling, each practiced in a block, with an attending standing beside every intern and commenting on nearly every attempt. Interns left the boot camp exhausted and visibly better. After that, technical skill was learned where Pruitt believed it belonged — in the operating room, under graduated autonomy, with attendings deciding case by case how much each resident could do. Attendings rated residents at the end of each rotation.

The model had deep support. Senior attendings liked it because it respected their judgment and their time. Residents liked the boot camp; it was one of the highest-rated events of the year. Pruitt was respected, persuasive and, not incidentally, responsible for the operating-room schedule on which every resident’s case volume depended.
The Skills Pathway

Dr. Sun-Hee Park, a surgeon who had trained in surgical education before joining Varnholt three years earlier, had proposed an alternative she called the Skills Pathway. Instead of two days in July, interns would attend weekly 45-minute sessions throughout their first year. Tasks would be mixed within sessions rather than practiced in blocks. Attending feedback would be frequent at first and then faded, with more emphasis on interns judging their own performance from video. Each skill would be checked by a blinded video assessment four and twelve weeks after it was introduced, and interns would need to reach a defined standard on certain skills before performing those steps in the operating room.

Park was careful in how she described the evidence. She cited research on spaced and retrieval-based practice and on the gap between performance during training and what is retained later. She also acknowledged that most motor-learning studies were laboratory experiments and that some principles she drew on were contested. “I’m not claiming the Pathway is proven,” she had told Abara. “I’m claiming the boot camp is designed to look good on the day, and nobody has ever checked what interns retain in October.”
The pilot

Last year, Abara had allowed a pilot. Of sixteen interns, eight volunteered for the Pathway; the other eight attended the boot camp and then followed the usual model. The results, summarized in Exhibit 1, had been discussed at three faculty meetings without agreement.

At the end of their first four hours of skills practice — two days for the boot-camp group, two weeks of sessions for the Pathway group — instructors rated the boot-camp interns substantially higher. Twelve weeks into the year, on a blinded video assessment of the practiced skills, the Pathway group scored higher, and the gap was smaller but in the same direction on a task neither group had practiced. Attending ratings of operating-room performance at three months were nearly identical. Pathway interns had reported lower confidence early on, and several had described the sessions as frustrating.

Park read the pilot as encouraging: the blinded retention and transfer measures favored the Pathway, while the measure that favored the boot camp was taken at the moment practice ended. Pruitt read it differently. “The only measure that happens in the real world is the operating-room rating, and it shows no difference,” he said at the last meeting. “The video scores come from eight volunteers who chose the new thing because they were keen. And they practiced nearly twice as many hours. Of course they scored higher on a video test of the thing they practiced.” He had a point, and Abara knew it. The Pathway interns had accumulated 31 hours of structured practice by week twelve, against 16 for the boot-camp group, because the boot camp ended in July while the Pathway sessions continued.
Pressures from three directions

The first pressure was safety. Last spring, an intern had struggled with a laparoscopic stapler during a night case. A senior resident took over, there was no harm to the patient, and the case review recorded the event as a near miss. The review noted, without assigning blame, that the intern’s only hands-on experience with that device had been at the July boot camp nine months earlier. Several attendings had quietly told Abara that the event was a fluke. Park had not said anything about it in public, which Abara suspected was deliberate.

The second was accreditation. A site visit was scheduled in ten months, and the reviewers were expected to ask how the program assessed technical competence. Rotation ratings by attendings were, in Abara’s honest view, not much of an answer: nearly everyone was rated “meets expectations” on nearly everything.

The third was money. Marcus Delgado, the finance director for the department, had been clear that the budget was flat. The Pathway would cost about $410,000 in its first year and about $257,000 a year after that, against $95,000 for the boot camp (Exhibit 2). Dropping the boot camp would cover part of the difference; the rest would have to come from somewhere else — the most likely candidates were an unfilled research coordinator position and the residents’ conference travel fund. Delgado did not have a view on surgical education. He did have a view on commitments that could not be reversed, and the simulation equipment was the largest single item.
The people who would have to make it work

The Pathway required six attendings to protect two hours a week. Abara could name four who would do it well and two who would do it because they were told to. Pruitt had not said he would oppose the program if it were adopted, but he had said that faculty time was “the scarcest thing in this building,” and everyone understood what he meant. Abara had seen mandated teaching before: sessions that started late, ended early and consisted of an attending checking a phone while interns practiced alone. A Pathway delivered that way might be worse than a boot camp delivered with conviction.

The chief residents were split. Priya Raman thought the Pathway was overdue; she remembered forgetting most of what she had learned in July by the time she needed it. Owen Feld worried about coverage. Taking every intern off the wards for 45 minutes a week meant the work fell to second- and third-year residents who were already near their duty-hour limits. “Everyone likes the idea of protected time,” he said. “Nobody likes being the person it’s protected from.”
What Abara did not know

Abara made a list of what she could not answer. She did not know whether better video scores in simulation would translate into better performance in the operating room, let alone better outcomes for patients. She did not know how much of the pilot’s difference came from spacing, how much from mixing tasks, how much from the extra practice hours, and how much from the fact that the volunteers were, perhaps, the interns most likely to improve anyway. She did not know whether the operating-room ratings showed no difference because there was none or because the ratings could not detect one. And she did not know whether the Pathway would survive contact with a faculty that had not chosen it.

She did know that the decision would be read as a verdict on Pruitt’s twenty-six years, whatever she intended, and that Okafor would ask her one question before any other: “If we do this and it doesn’t work, how will we know, and how fast?”

questions: What does the pilot actually show, and what can it not show? List at least three explanations for the week-twelve difference other than “the Pathway works better.”

Which outcome should carry the most weight in this decision — instructor ratings during training, blinded retention and transfer tests, attending operating-room ratings, or patient outcomes — and what would it cost to measure each well?
How should Abara involve Pruitt and the less enthusiastic attendings, given that they would have to deliver whatever is chosen?
Draft the recommendation Abara could defend in a fifteen-minute meeting with Okafor, including the result that would make you reverse it in twelve months.

perspectives.title: Adopt in phases, with a fair comparison
perspectives.text: Run the Pathway for half of next year’s interns, assigned at random, with equal total practice hours in both arms, leased equipment and blinded retention, transfer and operating-room assessments. Decide on full adoption after one year. This answers the confounds Pruitt raised, limits irreversible spending and gives the accreditation visit a credible assessment story. Its costs: a year’s delay, administrative effort, and the risk that a half-hearted control arm or a half-hearted Pathway arm biases the comparison.

perspectives.title: Keep the model; add the cheap, well-supported parts
perspectives.text: Retain the boot camp and operating-room apprenticeship, but add low-cost elements with the strongest evidence: brief spaced refresher sessions before rotations that use specific devices, short retrieval-based checks, and a blinded video assessment at twelve weeks for everyone. This respects faculty capacity and internal support, costs a fraction of the Pathway, and builds the measurement system the program lacks. Its weakness: it may preserve a massed design that the evidence suggests is weak for retention, and it postpones the larger question.

perspectives.title: Adopt the Pathway now
perspectives.text: The near miss, the accreditation question and the retention data all point the same way, and every year of delay sends another cohort into the operating room with skills learned nine months earlier. The evidence on spacing and retention is strong enough to act on, and perfect evidence will never come. The risks are real: a mandated program delivered by unwilling faculty, an irreversible equipment purchase, coverage strain, and a decision that will be read as defeating Pruitt.

perspectives.title: Fix measurement first
perspectives.text: The program cannot evaluate any training model because it cannot measure technical competence: operating-room ratings do not discriminate. Spend the next year building a blinded assessment system, applied to the current model, and decide afterward. This is the most defensible epistemically and the least confrontational, but it may look like avoidance, and it leaves the identified retention gap untouched for another cohort.

case.application: Player development departments face this choice constantly: a new practice system, technology or curriculum with an evidence-informed rationale and a higher cost, against an established process that staff trust and that seems to produce good players. The same traps apply. Practice-session data favor massed, blocked, guided designs; small pilots are confounded by volunteers and unequal practice volume; game outcomes are too noisy and delayed to judge a training change quickly; and the coaches who would deliver the new system are the people whose expertise it implicitly questions. The transferable moves are the ones this case invites: separate what the evidence supports from what is hypothesis, design a fair comparison with equal practice volume, measure retention and transfer rather than only practice performance, keep commitments reversible, and give the defenders of the current system a real role in testing its replacement.

questions.prompt: A fictional bank compared two compliance-training formats. Which interpretation of the results is best supported?

stimulus.text: Fictional study. 120 new employees were randomly assigned to Format A (one four-hour session; read the policy manual twice and highlight key rules) or Format B (four one-hour weekly sessions, each beginning with a short quiz on earlier material before review).

stimulus.caption: Results (synthetic)
stimulus.note: Synthetic data for a fictional study.

options.text: Format A is better because it produced higher immediate scores and higher satisfaction.
Format B produced more durable learning; judging by the immediate test would have picked the wrong format.
Format B is better, and the study shows that spacing alone caused the difference.
No conclusion is possible because satisfaction differed between the formats.

questions.explanation: The delayed test is the measure of learning, and it favors Format B by a wide margin, while the immediate test and satisfaction favor Format A — the crossover pattern described in the learning–performance literature. Because Format B combined spacing and retrieval quizzes, the study cannot say which component produced the benefit.

optionFeedback.a: Immediate scores and satisfaction are performance and experience measures; they often favor the less effective format.
optionFeedback.c: Format B differed from A in both spacing and retrieval practice (and in reading/highlighting), so the study cannot attribute the effect to spacing alone.
optionFeedback.d: Satisfaction is an outcome, not a confound; randomization makes the delayed-test comparison interpretable.

questions.prompt: An analyst is learning a new valuation method over three weeks. Which practices would add DESIRABLE difficulty? Select all that apply.

options.text: Begin each session by reconstructing last week’s steps from memory before checking the guide.
Reread the step-by-step guide three times before starting each problem.
Spread the six hours of training across three weeks instead of one day.
Mix problems that require different methods so the analyst must decide which applies.
Assign problems far beyond the analyst’s current ability, with no feedback.
Highlight the key passages of the manual.

questions.explanation: Retrieval before checking, spacing and interleaving all make practice harder in ways that support durable learning. Rereading and highlighting are low-utility techniques that create familiarity, and impossible tasks without feedback are undesirable difficulty: the learner cannot succeed, so the effort teaches little.

questions.prompt: You lead a training function. End-of-course scores for a new client-service program are very high, and your finance partner proposes cutting the planned 30-day follow-up test to save money. The program will be rolled out to 2,000 employees next quarter. What is the best next move?

options.text: Agree; the end-of-course scores already show the program works.
Keep a short, unannounced delayed test for a random sample of participants, and state in advance what result would change the rollout.
Replace the follow-up test with a satisfaction survey, which is cheaper and covers more people.
Add more questions to the end-of-course test to make it more rigorous.

questions.explanation: End-of-course scores measure performance, which can be high when little is retained. A delayed test on a random sample is cheap relative to a 2,000-person rollout and is the only option that measures learning; stating the decision rule in advance prevents the result from being explained away.

optionFeedback.a: Immediate scores can rank programs in the wrong order; they do not show retention.
optionFeedback.c: Satisfaction measures experience, which tends to favor easier, less effective training.
optionFeedback.d: A longer immediate test is still an immediate test; rigor does not substitute for delay.

questions.prompt: Identify the most serious flaw in this argument.

stimulus.text: “Our analysis of 300 engineers shows that top performers logged twice as many hours on our internal learning platform as everyone else. Research shows that expertise comes from ten thousand hours of deliberate practice. Therefore, requiring every engineer to log more platform hours will turn more of them into top performers.” — fictional internal memo

options.text: It treats a correlation as causal (stronger engineers may log more hours, or a third factor may drive both) and equates logged hours with deliberate practice.
Three hundred engineers is too small a sample to detect any relationship.
It cites research, and research is never relevant to individual companies.
It ignores that the top performers might simply have been lucky in their assignments.

questions.explanation: The memo moves from a correlation to a causal policy without ruling out reverse causation or confounding, and it equates platform hours with deliberate practice, which is defined by targeted, effortful, feedback-rich work. It also leans on the popular ten-thousand-hour rule, which misreads the original research.

optionFeedback.b: Three hundred is a reasonable sample for detecting a correlation; the problem is the inference drawn from it.
optionFeedback.c: Research can be relevant; the problem is that this research is misread and misapplied.
optionFeedback.d: Luck is one possible confound, but the central flaw is the causal leap and the misdefinition of practice.

questions.prompt: A study reports a correlation of r = .45 between accumulated practice and performance. What percentage of the variance in performance does practice explain? Give a percentage to two decimal places.
questions.working: For a single predictor, variance explained equals the square of the correlation: R² = r × r = 0.45 × 0.45 = 0.2025, or 20.25%. The remaining 79.75% of the differences in performance are associated with other factors or measurement error.
questions.explanation: Squaring the correlation converts it into the share of variance explained. A correlation that sounds substantial (.45) corresponds to about a fifth of the variance — similar to the figure reported for practice in sport overall.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation of this finding?

stimulus.text: A fictional professional soccer academy analyzes its 40 top-tier players, all of whom train full time. Accumulated training hours do not predict which players later sign professional contracts. The academy director proposes cutting training time by 25% across the academy, arguing that “the data show practice does not matter.”

options.text: The director is right; practice is irrelevant once players reach the top tier.

The finding reflects range restriction among players who all train heavily; it does not show that practice is unimportant, and any change should be tested on practice quality rather than imposed on volume.
The academy should increase training hours, because more practice always helps.
The analysis must be wrong, because practice obviously matters.

questions.explanation: When everyone in a sample trains heavily, differences in hours barely vary and cannot predict much — the same pattern as the elite-level result in the sport meta-analysis. The finding says hours do not distinguish these players; it does not say what would happen if training were cut. The defensible response is to test changes, especially in practice quality.

optionFeedback.a: A weak predictor within a restricted sample says nothing about the effect of reducing the predictor for everyone.
optionFeedback.c: The evidence does not show that more hours help these players either; it suggests hours are not what distinguishes them.
optionFeedback.d: A null correlation within a restricted range is expected and is not evidence of a flawed analysis.

questions.prompt: Rank these claims from STRONGEST to WEAKEST current evidential support, based on this week’s sources.

options.text: Random practice improves transfer of motor skills in applied sport settings.
Retrieval practice improves delayed retention of studied knowledge.
Random practice improves retention and transfer of laboratory motor tasks.
Matching instruction to learners’ preferred sensory style improves learning.

questions.explanation: Retrieval practice is rated high utility across a broad body of work. The laboratory contextual-interference effect is consistent, with a medium-to-large transfer effect in laboratory studies. In applied settings the transfer effect was small and not statistically significant, and one meta-analysis calls the benefit a myth. The learning-styles matching hypothesis lacks the crossover evidence it requires.

questions.prompt: A coach returning from a workshop wants to run every session for a group of novices with fully random practice and minimal feedback, “because the research says so.” The novices cannot yet perform the basic movement consistently. What is the best course of action?

options.text: Implement the workshop design for everyone immediately; research findings apply to all learners.
Begin with more blocked practice and more frequent feedback until the basic pattern is stable, then progressively mix tasks and fade feedback, and add a weekly cold check to see whether it works.
Reject the idea entirely, because contextual interference has been called a myth.
Let each novice choose their own schedule and feedback.

questions.explanation: Difficulty is desirable only when the learner can eventually succeed, and the evidence suggests the benefits of high interference depend on learner stage and are weaker in applied settings. A progressive design calibrates difficulty and guidance to skill, and a cold check turns the change into a testable hypothesis.

optionFeedback.a: Applied benefits are smaller and uncertain, and for learners without a stable pattern random practice is more likely to overload than to help.
optionFeedback.c: The applied evidence is contested, not settled against the principle; abandoning it entirely overcorrects.
optionFeedback.d: Learner choice may support engagement, but it does not address the calibration problem, and its learning benefits are uncertain.

questions.prompt: Two published meta-analyses of the same literature on attentional focus report the results summarized below. What should a coaching director conclude?

stimulus.caption: Summary of two meta-analyses of external versus internal focus
rows: Not the focus of the conclusion
Moderate to strong evidence in every analysis; Bayes factors favor no effect
stimulus.note: Figures as reported by Chua et al. (2021) and McKay et al. (2024).

options.text: Trust the 2021 analysis, because it is the original and was conducted by experts in the field.
The average benefit of external cues is uncertain; they are cheap and low-risk to use, but should not be taught as an established principle or used to justify bigger decisions.
External cues are harmful and should be banned from coaching.
The disagreement shows that meta-analysis is useless, so coaches should rely on their own experience.

questions.explanation: When a bias-corrected reanalysis of the same studies shrinks the effect toward zero, the honest conclusion is uncertainty. Bias corrections have assumptions of their own, so the result does not prove external cues never help; it means the principle cannot be presented as established. Because external cues cost little, using them as a default while not overselling them is reasonable.

optionFeedback.a: Being first or authored by proponents does not protect a literature from publication bias; the reanalysis used the same studies.
optionFeedback.c: Neither analysis found harm; the dispute is whether there is a reliable benefit.
optionFeedback.d: The disagreement is informative: it shows how publication bias can inflate effects. Personal experience is subject to the same fluency illusions this week describes.

questions.prompt: A vendor’s brochure for a fictional athlete-development platform makes the claims below. Select EVERY claim that should be challenged before purchase.

options.text: The platform profiles each athlete’s learning style and matches drills to it.
Its puzzle games improve on-field decision speed.
Playbook content is reviewed through spaced retrieval quizzes.
Success is shown as rising accuracy on the platform’s in-app drills.
High-repetition drills “build motor engrams” that guarantee consistency.
Delayed retention tests are built in, and results can be exported.

questions.explanation: Learning-style matching lacks supporting evidence; improvement from puzzle games to on-field decisions is a far-transfer claim that should be tested directly; rising in-app accuracy is a performance measure under practice conditions; and “building engrams” is an unfalsifiable neuroscience gloss. Spaced retrieval for knowledge content and exportable delayed retention tests are well-supported features.

questions.prompt: A hospital is considering a commercial brain-training app to improve residents’ clinical reasoning. Which judgment is best supported by evidence on transfer?

options.text: Adopt it; general cognitive training reliably improves performance in specialized professional tasks.
Be skeptical: far transfer from general training to distant tasks is rare, so invest first in practice on clinical reasoning cases themselves and test any app directly against that.
Adopt it only for residents who are visual learners.
Reject all training technology, since transfer never occurs.

questions.explanation: Reviews of chess, music and working-memory training find that far transfer to general abilities is rare and shrinks in better-controlled studies. Near transfer — practicing reasoning on cases like the real ones — is far more likely to help. Any claim of far transfer should be tested against that alternative.

optionFeedback.a: This asserts far transfer, which the evidence suggests is rare.
optionFeedback.c: Learning-style matching lacks supporting evidence and does not address the transfer problem.
optionFeedback.d: Near transfer is common; technology that practices the target task can help. The problem is distance, not technology.

questions.prompt: Choose one skill that matters in your work (technical, physical or professional). In 150–250 words, design a measurement plan that would let you tell, within three months, whether a new practice design is producing learning rather than only better practice performance. Name the measures, when they are taken, what you will deliberately NOT treat as evidence of learning, and the result that would make you abandon the new design.
questions.modelAnswer: Skill: a second-year analyst’s ability to build a defensible valuation model. Current practice: worked examples followed by similar problems. New design: spaced sessions that open with retrieval and mix problem types. Measures: (1) a short, unannounced cold problem at the start of each fortnight, before any review, scored by a reviewer who does not know which design the analyst received; (2) a transfer problem every six weeks using an industry not covered in training; (3) error rates on real deliverables, tracked but treated as noisy. Not evidence of learning: accuracy on in-session practice problems, the analyst’s confidence, and the trainer’s impression of the sessions, because all three are inflated by easier designs. Comparison: if possible, half of the cohort, assigned at random, continues the old design, with equal total practice time. Decision rule, stated in advance: if after three months the cold-check and transfer scores are not at least as good for the new design, revert, since it costs more trainer time; if they are clearly better, extend it and keep the checks running.

rubric.criterion: Separates learning measures (delayed, changed-context) from performance measures
levels: 0 — relies on in-session or immediate measures
1 — includes a delayed or transfer measure but also treats practice performance as evidence
3 — clear delayed and transfer measures, and explicitly excludes practice performance and confidence
2 — a comparison group or schedule, ideally with equal practice time
2 — specific result that would trigger reverting or continuing

rubric.criterion: Feasibility and fit to the chosen skill
levels: 1 — realistic for the skill and setting

reserve.prompt: In the testing-effect experiments, students who restudied a passage rather than taking recall tests were MORE confident about remembering it. Why does this finding matter for training design?

options.text: It shows that confident learners always remember more.
It shows that learners’ sense of progress can favor the less effective method, so their preferences and confidence are poor guides to how to practice.
It shows that testing reduces motivation and should be avoided.
It shows that restudying and testing are equally effective.

reserve.explanation: Restudying produced more confidence and worse delayed retention. Fluency during study feels like learning, so learner confidence and satisfaction can systematically favor weaker methods. Training designers need delayed measures, not only learner judgments.

optionFeedback.a: The opposite occurred: the more confident group remembered less after a delay.
optionFeedback.c: The study measured confidence, not motivation, and testing improved long-term retention.
optionFeedback.d: Restudying won on an immediate test, but testing won on delayed tests.

reserve.prompt: What is the strongest version of the argument this coach is making, and its main weakness?

stimulus.text: A fictional conservatory teacher argues: “Those meta-analyses averaged everything from casual rehearsal to group lessons and called it deliberate practice. When you look only at individualized practice designed by a teacher, practice explains far more of the difference between students.”

options.text: It mirrors Ericsson and Harwell’s definitional argument; its weakness is that the supporting reanalysis rests on a small, selected set of studies and corrections that can inflate estimates.
It shows that the meta-analyses were fraudulent; it has no weakness.
It is an argument that talent is innate; its weakness is that practice obviously matters.
It is irrelevant to the debate because it concerns music rather than sport.

reserve.explanation: This is the definitional rebuttal: the meta-analyses counted structured practice, and studies matching the original definition show larger effects. The reanalysis, however, uses a small subset of studies and attenuation corrections that depend on uncertain reliability estimates, so its larger figures should be held loosely.

optionFeedback.b: Disagreement about definitions is not evidence of fraud, and the argument has real limitations.
optionFeedback.c: The teacher argues that practice matters more than the meta-analyses suggest, not that talent is innate.
optionFeedback.d: The deliberate-practice debate spans music, games, sport, education and professions; the definitional point applies across them.

reserve.prompt: Which statements accurately describe the 2024 meta-analysis of contextual interference and transfer discussed this week? Select all that apply.

options.text: Overall, random practice was favored with a medium effect on transfer.
In applied settings, the effect was small and not statistically significant.
The effect was larger in laboratory studies than in applied settings.
In young participants, the effect was especially large.
It proved that contextual interference is a myth.

reserve.explanation: The meta-analysis found a medium overall effect (SMD = 0.55), a larger and significant laboratory effect (0.75), a small non-significant applied effect (0.34) and a negligible effect in young participants (0.12). It is a different research group that argues the applied benefit is a myth.

reserve.prompt: A training lead reconciles two pieces of advice: “reduce cognitive load” and “add desirable difficulties.” Which reconciliation is best?

options.text: They contradict each other; choose one philosophy and apply it consistently.
Cut load created by poor presentation (too many cues, redundant information) and add productive difficulty (retrieval, spacing, mixing once basics are stable), calibrated to the learner’s expertise.
Reduce load for experts and add difficulty for novices.
Add as much difficulty as possible, because harder practice always produces more learning.

reserve.explanation: Extraneous load comes from how information is presented and should be cut; productive difficulty comes from what the learner must retrieve, space or choose and can be added in doses the learner can handle. Because methods that help novices can become redundant for experts, the calibration depends on expertise.

optionFeedback.a: The two ideas address different sources of difficulty and are compatible.
optionFeedback.c: This reverses the expertise logic: novices generally need more guidance and less added difficulty than experts.
optionFeedback.d: Difficulty is desirable only when the learner can eventually succeed; too much becomes undesirable.

assignment.title: An Evidence-Informed Development Framework

brief.text: Write a framework that a player development department could adopt to guide how skills are practiced, coached and measured. The framework should be general enough to apply across positions and levels, and specific enough that a new coach could use it to design a week of practice. It must contain no confidential or club-specific material; describe a fictional or generic organization.

The defining requirement is honesty about evidence. Every principle in your framework must carry a label: **Supported** (consistent evidence, including outside the laboratory where relevant), **Contested** (credible evidence on both sides, or effects that shrink under scrutiny), **Coaching hypothesis** (plausible, drawn from experience or theory, not yet tested) or **Not supported** (claims the framework explicitly rejects). A framework that labels everything “Supported” will score poorly, however persuasive it is.

items: Cite this week’s sources where you rely on research, and state the strength of the evidence in your own words.
Include at least one element you would test in your own organization, with the measure and decision rule.
Address learner stage: how the framework changes for a beginner, a developing player and an established professional.
Write for two readers at once: the head of the department, who needs the logic and the risks, and a coach, who needs to know what to do on Monday.

brief.text: Before drafting, list the five practice habits most common in the environments you know best. You will need to place each in your evidence ledger.

assignment.deliverable: A 1,400–2,000-word development framework with an evidence ledger that labels each principle Supported, Contested, Coaching hypothesis or Not supported.

template.heading: Purpose, scope and learners
template.guidance: Which skills and levels the framework covers, and what “development” means here — learning that is retained and transfers to competition, not practice success.

template.heading: Core principles
template.guidance: Five to eight principles, each with its evidence label and a one-sentence rationale citing this week’s sources where relevant.

template.heading: Practice design by learner stage
template.guidance: Scheduling (blocked, serial, random, progressive), spacing, variability and representative design for beginners, developing players and established professionals.

template.heading: Feedback and coaching language
template.guidance: Feedback frequency and type, how it fades, cue policy (one cue at a time; how external and analogy cues are used without overselling them) and how coaches avoid overloading working memory.

template.heading: Measuring learning
template.guidance: A measurement calendar with retention (cold) checks and transfer checks; which data you will not treat as evidence of learning; how competition data are used despite their noise.

template.heading: Evidence ledger
template.guidance: A table of every element: label, source or basis, and what evidence would change its label. Include at least two items you reject as Not supported.

template.heading: Implementation, coach development and review
template.guidance: How coaches learn the framework, one pilot you would run (with comparison, equal practice volume, measures and decision rule), and when the framework is reviewed.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Every research claim is accurate and appropriately cited; labels match the evidence, including laboratory–applied gaps and bias-corrected results.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Claims are accurate with minor overstatement; most labels are well matched.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Some claims are overstated or mislabelled (for example, contested principles presented as settled).

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Frequent inaccuracies or unsupported claims presented as research.

rubric.criterion: Quality of practice and feedback design

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Design is specific, coherent and calibrated by learner stage; difficulty, variability and feedback move together with skill.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Design is sound and specific, with some stage differentiation.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Design is generic or applies one prescription to all learners.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Little actionable design; principles are not translated into practice.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Clear retention and transfer measures on a realistic calendar; explicitly excludes practice performance and confidence as evidence of learning; includes a pilot with a comparison and decision rule.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Includes delayed and transfer measures and a plausible pilot, with minor gaps.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Relies mainly on practice or game data; delayed measures are vague.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No meaningful plan to distinguish learning from performance.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: The ledger is complete and candid; hypotheses are named as such, with tests that could change them; at least two popular claims are rejected with reasons.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Most elements are labelled honestly; tests are proposed for some hypotheses.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Labels are present but uneven; hypotheses are often presented as findings.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No meaningful distinction between evidence and belief.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: A department head and a coach could both act on it; costs, staff capacity and risks are addressed concisely.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Clear and usable, with some gaps on cost or capacity.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Usable by one audience but not the other; feasibility is assumed.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Hard to follow or impractical.

prompts: Think of the skill you have taught or coached most often. Describe the practice design you default to — schedule, feedback, cues, measurement. Which parts did you choose because of evidence, and which because that is how you were taught?
Recall a time you judged someone’s progress from what you saw in practice and later found you were wrong. What signal misled you, and what would you measure differently now?
Which belief about talent, practice or feedback did this week challenge most for you? Write down the evidence that would make you abandon it completely — and the evidence that would make you keep it.

Apply the week to yourself: schedule three short retrieval sessions on this week’s material over the next three weeks, without rereading first. What do you predict you will remember, and how confident are you?

review.front: What is the difference between learning and performance?
review.back: Performance is what a learner does during or right after practice. Learning is a relatively permanent change that supports retention and transfer, so it must be inferred from delayed or changed-context tests.

review.front: In the testing-effect experiments, which condition won on the five-minute test, and which after one week?
review.back: Restudying won at five minutes; testing won after two days and one week. Restudiers were also more confident despite remembering less.

review.front: Which two techniques received high utility ratings in the review of ten learning techniques? Which two popular ones were rated low?
review.back: High: practice testing and distributed practice. Low (among others): rereading and highlighting.
When it slows acquisition but improves retention or transfer and the learner can eventually succeed. Difficulty that prevents success, or comes from poor presentation, is undesirable.

review.front: Why does interleaving help when the real task involves recognizing the situation?
review.back: Mixing problem types forces the learner to choose the right approach on each item, which blocked practice never requires.

review.front: Define deliberate practice in its original sense.
review.back: Effortful, individualized practice designed (often by a teacher) to improve a specific weakness, with immediate feedback and repetition with refinement — not simply time on task.

review.front: About how much of the variance in performance did deliberate practice explain in sport overall, and among elite athletes?
review.back: About 18% overall and about 1% among elite athletes (Macnamara, Moreau and Hambrick, 2016).

review.front: Why can a variable matter a great deal yet explain little variance among elite performers?
review.back: Range restriction: if everyone in the sample has a lot of it, it barely varies and cannot predict differences among them.

review.front: What is Ericsson and Harwell’s central objection to the deliberate-practice meta-analyses?
review.back: They counted structured practice in general rather than deliberate practice as originally defined; studies matching the definition show larger effects. The reanalysis rests on a small, selected set of studies.

review.front: What did Shea and Morgan (1979) find for blocked versus random practice?
review.back: Blocked practice was better during acquisition; random practice was better for retention (especially under random testing) and transfer.

review.front: What happens to the contextual interference effect in applied settings, according to the 2024 transfer meta-analysis?
review.back: It was small and not statistically significant (SMD 0.34), versus 0.75 in the laboratory; negligible in young participants. Another meta-analysis calls the applied benefit a myth.

review.front: What does the guidance hypothesis predict about feedback after every attempt?
review.back: Better practice performance but weaker retention, because the learner comes to depend on augmented feedback rather than their own error detection.

review.front: What is the status of the external-focus advantage?
review.back: Contested: a 2021 meta-analysis reported medium learning effects; a 2024 bias-corrected reanalysis found effects near zero with Bayes factors favoring no effect.

review.front: How does a constraints-led coach change a practice?
review.back: By manipulating task, environment and individual constraints (space, rules, equipment, opponents) so solutions emerge, rather than prescribing and correcting one technique.

review.front: What is the expertise reversal effect?
review.back: Methods that help novices, such as detailed guidance and worked examples, can become redundant or harmful for more expert learners.

review.front: What evidence would be needed to support the learning-styles matching hypothesis?
review.back: Learners classified by style, randomly assigned to matched or mismatched instruction, the same test for all, and a crossover interaction. Such evidence has not been found.

preview.text: This week gave you a working rule: judge development by what lasts and transfers, and grade every claim before you build on it. Week 4 supplies the research-literacy tools behind that rule — statistical power, publication bias, effect sizes and causal inference — so you can read a meta-analysis such as the attentional-focus dispute on your own. Week 5 treats coaching and development as a social system in which credibility and relationships decide whether good ideas are adopted, and the later weeks on organizations and execution return to the problem in this week’s case: changing an established process that people trust.
